entries.note: The root box is right: Pokorny IEW 632 heads the article 'k̑uon-, k̑un- ‘Hund’; ursprüngl. Nom. Sg. k̑úuo(n), Gen. k̑unos', and Watkins/AHD has 'kwon-. Dog. [Pok. k̑uon- 632.]'. Nourai's three-part root name is his own shorthand for the three ablaut/stem shapes he collects under it: Kwon = the full grade *ḱwon- (Gk. kúōn, Gmc. *hundaz), Ka 2 = the Latin a-vocalism canis, Sua = the Indo-Iranian *ćwā- (Skt. śván-, Av. spā). All three are in Pokorny's article. The language label 'Indo-European' and the gloss 'dog' are correct. The one substantive problem on this page is not the root but a branch: the 'army' words (Av. spāδa-, OP spāda-, NP sepāh, Isfahan, Sogd. spʽδ) are hung under the dog root, and no modern authority — including Kent, whom Nourai cites for OP spāda- — accepts that; see nodes #4 and #7.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ هندواروپایی آغازین *ḱwṓ (کهن‌تر *ḱwón-s)، حالت اضافی *ḱunés، به معنی «سگ»؛ پوکورنی در فرهنگ ریشه‌شناسی هندواروپایی، ص ۶۳۲، همین ریشه را با همین معنا آورده و واتکینز (AHD) نیز آن را به همین صورت ثبت کرده است. سه‌نامی که نورایی برای ریشه آورده (Kwon، Ka 2، Sua) در واقع سه ستاکِ همان ریشه است: *ḱwon- (یونانی kúōn، ژرمنی *hundaz)، صورت لاتینی با a (canis) و ستاک هندوایرانی *ćwā- (سنسکریت śvan-، اوستایی spā). پس عنوان ریشه، برچسب زبانی و معنای آن هر سه درست است. اشکال اصلی این صفحه در خودِ ریشه نیست، بلکه در شاخه‌ای است که واژه‌های «سپاه» (اوستایی spāδa-، پارسی باستان spāda-، سغدی spʾδ، فارسی سپاه، اصفهان) را زیر ریشهٔ «سگ» نشانده است؛ هیچ منبع امروزی — حتی کِنت که خودِ نورایی به او ارجاع می‌دهد — این پیوند را نمی‌پذیرد (نگاه کنید به گره‌های ۴ و ۷).

nodes.derivation: Avestan spā (nom. sg.) 'dog', acc. spānəm, gen. pl. sūnąm — an athematic hysterokinetic n-stem continuing PIE nom. *ḱwṓ, gen. *ḱunés; the strong stem gives spā/spān-, the weak stem sūn- (PIE *ḱun- > Ir. *śun- > Av. sūn-), so Nourai's pair 'spâ 1, sŭnô' is the correct nom./gen. couple of one paradigm. Bartholomae AiW s.v. 'j. ¹span- : spā m. ‘Hund’' documents both, with the Pahlavi gloss sak and 'ai. śvā ... np. vgl. sag'. spakā is not, strictly, Avestan-and-Old-Persian: it is the Median form σπάκα that Herodotus I.110 reports ('the Medes call the dog spaka'), a *ḱun-ko- adjective 'dog-like' substantivised; Avestan has the matching adjective spaka- 'hundeartig, Hunds-' (Vd. 14.5), and Bartholomae's entry for it explicitly cross-refers to Herodotus. The label is therefore a shade loose — Old Persian has no attested word for 'dog' at all — but the forms and the descent from the root are right.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian sag, written with the Aramaic heterogram KLBʾ (from Aram. kalbā 'dog'), and in Book-Pahlavi transcription often given as sak because Pahlavi script does not distinguish g from k. MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary prints 'sag [KLBAʾ < A klb | N ~] dog'. The form is the south-western Iranian outcome of the same n-stem: the weak stem *ću(n)- with the -ka- suffix that the Median form also shows, i.e. OIr. *sa(n)ka- > MP sag; Iranian *ć- gives Persian s- (against the sp- of Avestan/Median/Pashto), so sag and spaka are the SW and NW reflexes of one word. Nourai's 'sak' is thus a legitimate transliteration of the Pahlavi spelling, not an error; Pokorny writes the same 'mpers. sak'.

nodes.derivation: New Persian سگ sag 'dog' continues Middle Persian sag unchanged — the commonest of all Persian animal names, in the Shahnameh and every later text. The whole chain is uncontroversial: PIE *ḱwṓ / weak stem *ḱun- > Proto-Iranian *ćwā / *ću(n)-ka- > SW Old Iranian *saka- > MP sag (KLBʾ) > NP سگ. The sp-/s- doublet survives beside it in the Iranian dialects Horn lists (Kurd. seh, Talishi sipā, Kashani espa/esbe, Semnani asp-), so Persian s- against Avestan sp- is the regular South-Western treatment of Ir. *ć and not a difficulty. The Arabic-looking سگ has nothing Semitic about it; the Pahlavi heterogram KLBʾ is a writing convention only.
nodes.derivation_fa: فارسی نو «سگ» دنبالهٔ بی‌تغییرِ فارسی میانهٔ sag است؛ رایج‌ترین نام جانور در فارسی، از شاهنامه تا امروز. زنجیرهٔ آن بی‌مناقشه است: هندواروپایی *ḱwṓ (ستاک ضعیف *ḱun-) < ایرانی آغازین *ćwā / *ću(n)-ka- < ایرانی باستانِ جنوب‌غربی *saka- < پهلوی sag < فارسی «سگ». جفتِ sp-/s- هنوز در گویش‌های ایرانی زنده است — کردی seh، تالشی sipā، کاشانی espa/esbe، سمنانی asp- — که هرن و به‌پیروی از او معین در حاشیهٔ برهان قاطع فهرست کرده‌اند؛ پس s فارسی در برابر sp اوستایی، تحول قاعده‌مندِ *ć ایرانی در شاخهٔ جنوب‌غربی است، نه استثنا. هزوارشِ KLBʾ در پهلوی صرفاً قرارداد نگارشی است و ربطی به سامی‌بودن واژه ندارد. ادعای نورایی در این گره کاملاً درست است.

An independent Borhan witness to the same word from the other side of the alphabet: 'اسپه ... مخفف اسپاه است که لشکر و سپاه باشد - و سگ را نیز گویند که بتازی کلب خوانند، و با پای فارسی هم گفته‌اند' — Borhan itself records that اسپه means both 'army' and 'dog', i.e. it preserves the sp-form of the dog word beside the homophonous army word.

nodes.derivation: The words are all genuine and Nourai's internal chain is right; what is wrong is hanging them on the dog root. Avestan spāδa- m. 'army' (Nourai's 'spâda, spâtha' is one word in two transliterations of the interdental δ), spāδa-paiti- 'army-chief' and the toponym behind Ptolemy's Aspadána are all built on spāδa-. But Avestan sp- here is not the sp- of spā 'dog': it goes back to Proto-Iranian *ćwāHda- < PIE *ḱweh₁-dʰ-o- from the root *ḱweh₁-/*ḱewh₁- 'to swell, be great' — the root of Av. sūidiiāi 'to swell, increase', Bactrian σοδο 'plenty', Skt. śávas- 'strength', MP sūd 'profit'. The semantic development is 'swelling, mass' → 'host, army'. Kent, whom Nourai himself cites for the Old Persian member (KNT:210), writes 'Possibly from pIE *k̑wō- ‘swell, be great’ (Gray, Lg. 25.377-8)'; Bartholomae likewise refers the group to an Aryan *sphā-. Pokorny p.632, Nourai's other reference, treats k̑uon- 'Hund' and says nothing whatever about spāδa-. No modern authority derives 'army' from 'dog'. The chart's own placement is therefore a false etymology; each individual form in the box is nevertheless correctly given.

nodes.derivation: Taken as drawn from its own parent (the Avestan spāδa- box), this node is right in every part. (i) سپاه sepāh/sipāh 'army' < MP spāh [spʾh] < OIr. *spāda-; the intervocalic Iranian -δ- of Av. spāδa- is lost and compensated by -h in the Middle Persian form (MacKenzie 'spāh ... N sipah'), poetic سپه sepah being the shortened variant. Middle Persian actually borrowed the word from a north-western dialect, which is why it keeps sp- rather than showing the SW treatment. (ii) سپهبد sepahbod < MP spāhbed [spʾh-pt] < OIr. *spāda-pati- 'lord of the army', the Sasanian title of the four quarter-generals; Armenian borrowed it as sparapet from Parthian, and Arabic took it as iṣbahbad/isfahbad, whence it came back into Persian usage. سپهسالار is a later New Persian synonym (سپه + Ar.-Pers. سالار), not a continuation of the Old Iranian compound. (iii) اصفهان Esfahān < MP Spāhān < OIr. *spādānām '(place) of the armies', a genitive plural used as a place name; Ptolemy's Aspadána and Middle Persian Spāhān are the same name, and the Arabic-script اصفهان with ص and initial ا is the Arabised spelling of Isfahān. Only the ultimate attachment to the 'dog' root (node #4) is wrong.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian ʾspʾδ / spʾδ 'army' (read (o)spaδ, ispaδ), attested in the Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian corpora and in the Bugut inscription. It is the eastern-Iranian sister of Av. spāδa-, keeping the interdental δ that Middle Persian lost; the prothetic ʾ- before the sp- cluster is the ordinary Sogdian repair of initial sC-, so ʾspʾδ and spʾδ are one word in two spellings — which is exactly what Nourai's doublet 'sp`d, `spd' represents (his ` stands for aleph). Derivatives ʾspʾδβʾry 'army equipment' and ʾspʾδyʾn (pl.) are attested alongside. As with #4-#5, the word is correct; only its parentage under the dog root is not.

nodes.derivation: Old Persian spāda- 'army' is real — but attested only inside the Median personal name Taxmaspāda- (DB 2.78-91, the Mede sent against Ciçantaxma) and, at one remove, in spāθmaida- 'camp' (DNb 30f); the -sp- shows it is a Median (north-western) form taken into the Old Persian of the inscriptions, since native South-Western Persian would have *sāda-. Nourai's arrow, however, is drawn from node #1 (spā 'dog'), and that is what modern scholarship rejects: Kent, the very reference cited here, writes s.v. späda- 'GAv. spāda-, NPers. sipah ... Possibly from pIE *k̑wō- ‘swell, be great’', and elsewhere lists späda- among the OP words 'only in Iranian'. Wiktionary derives the whole family from Proto-Iranian *ćwāHdah < PIE *ḱweh₁-dʰ-o-, root *ḱweh₁- 'to swell, be great'. So the form and the language label are correct, the parent is not.

nodes.derivation: Old Persian Sakā is the name of the Scythians and of their province (DB 1.16f, DNa 25, DPe 18, DSe 24, XPh 26, DBk 2 'Skunkha the Scythian'); there is no Old Persian common noun sakā 'dog'. Nourai's gloss 'dog' therefore reports an etymology of the ethnonym, not a meaning. His reference does back him: Kent, Lexicon p.209 s.v. Saka-, adds 'Probably ‘dog’ in good sense, = ‘guardian of the flocks’, pIE *k̑uon-, Med. σπάκα ‘dog’ (Herod. 1.110), cf. Van Windekens, Beitr. z. Namenforschung 1.98-102.' The reconstruction is phonetically possible — an Old Iranian *saka- 'dog' is independently posited by Nyberg as the SW form standing behind Middle Persian sag, from the zero-grade *ću-n-ka- — so a homonymy between the tribal name and the dog word is not absurd. But it is a minority view and not the modern default: the ethnonym is more usually left unexplained or connected with a root *sak- 'to go, roam' (whence 'the roamers, nomads'), and Wiktionary's Persian سگ page derives the dog word from OP *sakah without identifying it with Sakā. Verdict: plausible, exactly as far as Kent takes it, and no further.

nodes.derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaz 'dog' from PIE *ḱun-tó-, i.e. the zero grade of *ḱwṓ with a dental (-to-) enlargement; the initial *ḱ- gives Germanic h- by Grimm's Law, and the *-t- of the suffix is protected from the same shift by the preceding *n... Pokorny states the formation plainly at IEW 632-633: 'got. hunds, aisl. hundr, ags. hund, ahd. hunt ‘Hund’ (k̑un-tó-)'. Watkins puts it the same way: 'Suffixed zero-grade form *kwn-to- in Germanic *hundaz'. The chart's spelling 'hundaz' with the -az of the Germanic masculine a-stem nominative is the standard reconstruction. Descent from the root as drawn is correct.

nodes.derivation: Old English hund 'dog' (the general word until Middle English) > ME hund, hound > NE hound. The Middle English spelling with -ou- represents the regular lengthening/rounding of OE ū before the nasal cluster in the orthography of the Anglo-Norman scribes; the semantic narrowing from 'dog (any)' to 'hunting dog' happened in Middle English after the borrowing of dogge/dog into the general sense. The node has no reference in the book, but Klein's 'hound' article (the very page cited for the parent, KLN:746) and Skeat both carry the chain. Descent from Proto-Germanic *hundaz as drawn is correct.

nodes.derivation: Latin canis 'dog' belongs to the root, though with an irregularity everyone notes: the expected outcome of *ḱwon-/*ḱun- would be *cunis or the like, and the a of canis is unexplained — Pokorny writes 'ganz unklar lat. canis ‘Hund’ ... hinsichtlich des a; vielleicht Einmischung eines dem mir. cano, cana ‘Wolfsjunges’, cymr. cenaw entsprechenden Wortes'; Watkins simply files it as 'Variant *kan-i-'. So the membership is certain, the vocalism disputed. Insula Canaria is Pliny's name (Naturalis Historia VI.205) for the largest of the Fortunatae Insulae, 'so called from its multitude of dogs of a huge size' — Pliny reports that Juba II's expedition brought two of them back; hence Nourai's gloss 'dog island, named after its large dogs', which is Pliny's own explanation. (A rival modern theory takes the name from the Berber Canarii of the opposite Moroccan coast; Pliny's account is nevertheless the ancient one and the one that produced the Latin form.)
nodes.derivation_fa: لاتینِ canis «سگ» به همین ریشه تعلق دارد، هرچند با بی‌قاعدگی‌ای که همه یادآور شده‌اند: از *ḱwon-/*ḱun- انتظار *cunis می‌رفت و a در canis ناروشن است؛ پوکورنی می‌نویسد «لاتینِ canis از حیثِ a کاملاً ناروشن است؛ شاید آمیزشی با واژه‌ای همانندِ ایرلندیِ میانه cano/cana «تولهٔ گرگ» و ولزیِ cenaw رخ داده باشد»، و واتکینز آن را صرفاً «گونهٔ *kan-i-» می‌نامد. پس عضویتِ واژه در این خانواده قطعی است و تنها واکهٔ آن محلِّ بحث. Insula Canaria نامی است که پلینیِ بزرگ (تاریخ طبیعی، ۶٫۲۰۵) به بزرگ‌ترینِ «جزایرِ سعادت» داده و آن را «به سببِ انبوهیِ سگ‌های تنومندش» چنین خوانده است؛ او می‌افزاید که هیئتِ اعزامیِ یوبای دوم دو قلاده از آن سگ‌ها را با خود آورد. پس شرحِ نورایی («جزیرهٔ سگ، نامیده به‌سببِ سگ‌های بزرگش») همان توضیحِ خودِ پلینی است. (نظریهٔ رقیبِ امروزی نام را از قومِ بربرِ Canarii در ساحلِ مقابلِ مراکش می‌گیرد، اما صورتِ لاتینی از روایتِ پلینی برخاسته است.)

nodes.derivation: Two separate English descendants of the Latin box, both correct. (i) kennel 'dog-house' came into Middle English (c.1300 kenel) from Anglo-Norman/Old Northern French kenil, chenil, from Vulgar Latin *canile 'dog-house' — a -īle formation on canis exactly parallel to Latin ovīle 'sheepfold' from ovis and bovīle from bos; the Norman k- against Central French ch- is the regular Northern French retention of Latin c- before a, and is why English has kennel, not *chenel. (Klein separates it from the homonym kennel 'gutter', which is from L. canālis — the chart means the dog word.) (ii) Canary Islands is the English rendering of Latin Insulae Canariae, taken over through Spanish Islas Canarias; the English name is thus a direct calque-plus-borrowing of the Latin name in node #13, not a derivative of the bird. Both belong under canis.

nodes.derivation: Spanish canario is first the adjective/ethnonym 'of the Canary Islands' (Islas Canarias < L. insulae Canariae), and from the 16th century the name of the small finch of those islands, Serinus canaria, exported to the Peninsula by Spanish traders after the conquest of the archipelago (Gran Canaria 1483, Tenerife 1496). The bird is thus named after the islands and the islands after the dogs, so Nourai's gloss 'from Canary Islands < a bird >' is exactly right, and so is the arrow from the Latin box. The Spanish monopoly on the trade (only cocks were sold, to keep breeding to Spain) is what carried the word into every European language.

nodes.derivation: French canari (also canarie in the 16th c.) 'canary bird', borrowed from Spanish canario as the trade in the bird spread north from Seville; the French form drops the Spanish -o and is first recorded in the mid-16th century. Klein states the borrowing directly at p.230 ('F. canari, canarie, fr. Sp. canario'). French is then the immediate donor both for English canary (node #18) and, much later and via the francophone channels of the 19th-20th century, for Persian قناری (node #17), so Nourai's fork here is correctly placed. (The homonym canard 'duck; hoax' is a different word, from OF caner 'to cackle', and Klein keeps them apart in adjacent entries.)

(هم‌آوایش canard «مرغابی؛ خبر ساختگی» واژهٔ دیگری است از caner فرانسویِ کهن «قدقد کردن» و کلاین آن دو را در دو مدخلِ پیاپی جدا نگه داشته است.)

nodes.derivation: Persian قناری qanārī 'canary' is a modern European loan, from French canari, taken in with the bird itself in the Qajar period; Mo‘in's Farhang-e Fārsī marks the entry with the French source and explains the name from the islands: 'قناری ... اصل این پرنده از جزایر قناری است (وجه تسمیه به همین مناسبت است) و از آنجا به دیگر نقاط جهان از جمله ایران برده شده'. The Arabic-looking spelling with ق and ی is orthographic dressing of the French sound shape (q- for the foreign k-/c- before ā is the normal Persian and Ottoman rendering, cf. قهوه‌خانه-type spellings and قوطی); the word has no Arabic root and is not a Semitic q-n-r formation. It is therefore not a Persian→Arabic→Persian round trip but a straight Europeanism, and Nourai's arrow French→Persian is right.
nodes.derivation_fa: «قناری» در فارسی وام‌واژه‌ای اروپایی و نو است: از فرانسویِ canari، که همراه با خودِ پرنده در دورهٔ قاجار وارد شد. معین در فرهنگ فارسی مدخل را با نشانِ زبانِ فرانسه آورده و وجه تسمیه را از نامِ جزایر گرفته است: «قناری … اصل این پرنده از جزایر قناری است (وجه تسمیه به همین مناسبت است) و از آنجا به دیگر نقاط جهان از جمله ایران برده شده». املای عربی‌نمای آن با «ق» و «ی» صرفاً آرایشِ خطّی برای صورتِ آواییِ فرانسوی است؛ نوشتنِ q به‌جای k/c بیگانه پیش از ā در فارسی و عثمانی معمول است (مانند «قوطی»). این واژه ریشهٔ عربی ندارد و ساختِ سه‌حرفیِ سامیِ ق‌ن‌ر نیست. پس اینجا با معرّب و رفت‌وبرگشتِ فارسی←عربی←فارسی روبه‌رو نیستیم، بلکه با وام‌واژه‌ای یکسره اروپایی؛ و پیکانِ نورایی (فرانسوی ← فارسی) درست است.

nodes.derivation: English canary is attested from the 1570s as Canary-bird and from the 1650s shortened to canary, alongside canary (sack) 'the wine of the islands' from the 1580s — both from French canarie/canari, itself from Spanish canario. The English word therefore reaches the Latin insula Canaria and canis by the four-step route the chart draws, and 'canary' is one of the English words Watkins files under kwon-. The chart's arrow from the French box (rather than straight from Spanish) matches Klein and Etymonline, which both make French the immediate donor.
